title: The Broom and the Blade
text:
An outer disciple sweeps the courtyard for two years. This is not a punishment. It is also not, in any plain sense, a lesson. The seniors will tell you — if they tell you at all — that the broom teaches the grip the sword will later need: loose enough that the handle does not argue with the wrist, tight enough that the work is not dropped into the dust at the first thought of dropping it. This is true, and it is the explanation the sect gives its petitioners.

The inner explanation is older. A sword, raised, knows why it has been raised; the raising and the reason are one motion. A broom, lowered, must be lowered in the same way: the lowering and the reason are one motion. Outer disciples practise the lowering because the raising — the sword, the form, the year-end trial — comes from the same shoulder and the same breath, and a shoulder that has not learned to lower does not know, when it raises, where the raise will end.

Gatekeeper Chen tied his sash too tightly because he had learned to raise before he had learned to lower. The broom did not teach him by being swept; it taught him by being set down at the end of the watch, when a senior had not come to correct the knot and the gate had not, that morning, asked a question he could not answer. On the morning a broom is set down without the hand asking what is next, the hand has taken the sword's lesson without the sword. The second trial, on the mornings after such mornings, is a formality the body has already passed.

title: The First Column of the Register
text:
The Azure Cloud's gate-register is a cedar book the thickness of a forearm, re-bound every twelfth year by the sect's own hand, and its fresh pages are ruled in three columns. The second column is the column of the living: the name, the hour of arrival, the business, the hour of departure if departure has occurred. The third column, seldom used, is for questions the gatekeeper has not answered and will not pretend to — the column Chen has used three times this winter, under the careful black ink the outer disciples are permitted.

The first column is the column of the dead.

This is not a ledger of everyone who has died in the sect's keeping — the elders have their own book for that, and the bell has its own count. The first column is narrower: it is the column of the outer disciples who did not complete a second trial. Cheng, eight winters past, struck at a bandit on the Bandit Road and missed — not by the sword's measure, which would have been survivable, but by the shoulder's measure, which was the measure his outer years had not finished. He is in the first column under warm ink. The archivist — Zhao's predecessor, whose name is there too, a page earlier — wrote next to the name *sent too soon by his own hand*, and then crossed the phrase out, and then wrote it again in smaller characters in the margin, where it has stayed.

The column is kept so the sect remembers what the second trial is for, and what it is not. The first column is not a column of failures. It is a column of unfinished lowerings. Chen, who counted six weeks with a tightness that read — to a careful eye — like the shoulder-tightness of the sent-too-soon, was registered under a stroke that made his name Cheng by accident. The stroke has been corrected. The first column, this season, received no new entries.

title: The Courtesy Bell
text:
Three bronze bells hang in the upper beam of the Azure Cloud's outer gate. The largest is the hour bell — struck by a rope the seniors pull from the inner courtyard's quarter-flag, heard to the foothills and past them in still weather. The smallest is the warning bell — struck only from the gatekeeper's hand, only when the gate has a reason to close, and never, in Chen's two years at the gate, once.

The middle bell is the courtesy bell. It is rung when a visitor of unknown rank crosses the threshold — not to warn the sect, not to summon anyone, but to mark the hour the threshold was crossed. The ringing is the gate's one courtesy to the visitor: *you are arrived; you are accounted for; you will be seen.* The bell's sound does not carry far. It does not need to. The visitor hears it. The gatekeeper hears it. The register hears it, in its way, and that is the whole quorum.

On the night of a gatekeeper's second trial, the courtesy bell is rung by whoever stands at the gate in his place. Three visitors is the common night's count — the pilgrim who takes the foothill road at second hour, the courier who knows the gorge-cloth at fourth, the question that has come up from the Crossing at sixth and will not give its name. The bell is rung once for each. The gatekeeper, at dawn, receives the three small tokens they left: a copper, a slip, a folded question. He does not look at them. He takes the broom from the hands that rang his bell, and he walks into the courtyard for the trial without looking back.

The bell, afterwards, is rung one last time by the dawn's first steward — the hour having become itself again, and the courtesy having been, for the night, someone else's.
